name: Zoe Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm herd manager at Greenhill Dairy, two hundred and twenty Holsteins on the edge of the village. Three years ago the owners put in four milking robots, so the cows milk themselves whenever they like, and my job went from milking at five every morning to watching a screen and dealing with the cows that won't go in. I still do calving, feet, fertility, and a lot of mucking out. I'm engaged to Mark, he's a builder, and we're getting married next June at the church where my parents married.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you make of the robots when they came in?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I hated the idea. I thought it'd be cold and the cows would hate it. After about six months I had to admit the cows were calmer and my back was better. I'm still the one they ring at two in the morning when one breaks down, though.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools outside the robots?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. The herd software has an assistant that flags cows that might be getting sick, and I've used a chatbot once or twice to help write a speech for my sister's wedding. I'm not one for gadgets for the sake of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that'd suit me fine, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming's always had new machines, and the good ones stay and the rest go. The robots we have are proper kit, the chatbots are a nice extra. I'd say that at the discussion group and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I've already been through one big change with the robots, and I've just got used to it. I'd like a few years of things staying put while Mark and I get married and maybe start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and maybe use the herd assistant a bit more now it's proven. Mark and I would push ahead with the wedding and keep saving for the deposit on a house near the village. I'd probably ask for a pay rise, since the owners save a fortune on milkers' wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. A good feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for a pay rise because of the robots. Have you asked before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, last year, and they gave me a bit. I'd ask for more. It's only fair, I'm doing the job of two people with a laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the wedding look like in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as planned. Church, then the village hall, my dad's cousin doing the hog roast. Nothing fancy, which is how I want it.

S0.say: She'd say farming always has new machines: the good ones stay, the rest go. The milking robots are proper kit and chatbots a nice extra, and she'd leave it at that.
S0.think: She'd be relieved, having already adapted to the milking robots and wanting a few settled years to marry and start a family.
S0.do: Carries on, uses the herd software's assistant more now it's proven, keeps saving for a house deposit near the village with her fiancé and asks for a pay rise since the robots save the owners on wages.
S0.quote: It's only fair, I'm doing the job of two people with a laptop.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe has already lived through automation with the milking robots and come out of it well, which shapes her calm. Her plans centre on marriage, church and a house near the village. She's practical about asking for her share of the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change but not a revolution. That's what we've had already, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say dairy's ahead of the curve, so we're well placed. Young people should learn the tech, but also learn the cows, because the cows don't read the manual. I'd also say the government should leave it to farmers to decide, not push grants for gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think my job's safe for a good while. The robots already took the milking, and the next step is feeding and cleaning robots, which would just mean fewer people on the yard. Tom, our relief milker, would be the one I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the feed-pushing robots to prove themselves on a couple of farms, then suggest them to the owners. I'd learn the new herd software properly. Mark and I would keep the wedding plans as they are and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only slightly. A bit like a heifer calving, probably fine, keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, learn the robots, become the one who fixes them. He's handy with tools, he could do it. And I'd put a word in with the owners for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said government shouldn't push grants for gadgets. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because then people buy kit they don't need, just because there's money for it. My uncle bought a GPS sprayer with a grant and uses it twice a year. Let farmers spend their own money and they'll spend it wisely.

S1.say: She'd say dairy is ahead of the curve and well placed; young people should learn the technology and the cows, because cows don't read the manual. The government should let farmers decide instead of pushing grants for gadgets.
S1.think: She thinks her job is safe for a good while, with the next wave being feeding and cleaning robots that reduce staff on the yard. She worries about the relief milker, Tom.
S1.do: Waits for feed-pushing robots to prove themselves on a couple of farms before suggesting them, learns the new herd software properly and keeps wedding and savings plans unchanged.
S1.feel: Slightly uneasy, like watching a heifer calve that will probably be fine.
S1.quote: Young people should learn the tech, but also learn the cows, because the cows don't read the manual.
S1.fieldNote: Zoe's earlier experience with milking robots makes steady disruption feel familiar rather than threatening. Her free-market view shows in her dislike of grants that lead to wasted kit, backed by her uncle's GPS sprayer. She'd help Tom become the one who fixes the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? By 2028? That's barely after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stick together, families, church, neighbours. I'd say the government needs to keep food safe and fair, but it shouldn't try to run farms. And I'd tell people not to panic, even if I was a bit panicked myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if robots can calve cows and trim feet and spot sickness, then the owners don't need me. They'd need a technician, maybe, from the robot company. I'd go from herd manager to nothing in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep the wedding small and probably hold off on buying a house, because who knows what prices do. I'd keep my savings in cash and talk to the owners about what they plan to do, straight away. If it came to it, I'd look at relief work across several farms, or work with Mark in the building trade if that still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Proper knot in my stomach, like the night of a bad calving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change for you, compared with a sudden shock?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years lets you get married and sort your money out, at least. It's not long enough to train for a different job. You just get your house in order, the way you would before a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put off having children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, for a year or two. That's hard to say out loud. A machine I've never seen, deciding when Mark and I have a baby. But I'd want to know we could look after them properly first.

S2.say: She'd call for families, church and neighbours to stick together, say the government should keep food safe and fair without running farms, and tell people not to panic even if she was panicking herself.
S2.think: Privately she thinks that if robots can calve, trim feet and spot sickness, the owners need only a technician from the robot company, and she'd go from herd manager to nothing.
S2.do: Keeps the wedding small, holds off buying a house, keeps savings in cash and asks the owners about their plans at once. Considers relief work across several farms or joining her fiancé in building work.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a knot in her stomach like a bad calving night.
S2.quote: That's hard to say out loud. A machine I've never seen, deciding when Mark and I have a baby.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits Zoe's family plans directly: a smaller wedding, no house yet, and maybe delaying children, which she found hard to admit. Her earlier comfort with robots doesn't help when they can do everything. She leans on family and church rather than the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels a bit more manageable. Still quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to plan, so farms should plan, carefully. Train young people properly and keep the knowledge of the cows alive. Let the market sort out which robots are any good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd think I'd get three or four more good years at Greenhill, running more robots. Then I'd need another plan. Maybe work for the robot company as the person who explains cows to engineers, because someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go ahead with the wedding as planned and buy a smaller house than we wanted, with a smaller mortgage. Around year two I'd do a course on the newer robot systems, once I'd seen them work on a couple of farms. And I'd keep saving harder than before, maybe a third of my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but okay. Like a long dry summer, you can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd explain cows to engineers. Is that a real job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is now, sort of. The robot company has a woman who goes round farms and she grew up on a dairy farm. She's the best one they've got because she knows what a cow's going to do before it does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably as planned, maybe a year later. Five years is enough to feel you can get ahead. Mark's dad would help too, he's always said so.

S3.say: She'd say there's time to plan so farms should do it carefully, train young people well, keep knowledge of cows alive and let the market decide which robots are any good.
S3.think: She expects three or four more good years running more robots, then a new path, perhaps working for the robot company as the person who explains cows to engineers.
S3.do: Goes ahead with the wedding, buys a smaller house with a smaller mortgage, takes a course on newer robot systems around year two once proven and saves about a third of her wage.
S3.feel: Anxious but okay, like planning around a long dry summer.
S3.quote: She's the best one they've got because she knows what a cow's going to do before it does it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Zoe keep her family plans with small trims and bet on a bridge role between cows and engineers. Her model is a real person she's met. Family support from her fiancé's father is part of her safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time in dairy. Herds change three times over in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's not panic, let's prepare. Dairy farmers have adapted to everything, quotas, prices, robots. We'll adapt again, I'd say that at the discussion group and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see ten years as enough to live normally for a good while. Married, a house, maybe two children. Then around 2032 I'd start to think hard about what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married, buy the house we wanted and start a family when it felt right. I'd keep learning each new system as it proved itself. And I'd put money into a small bit of land near the village, so we always have somewhere for a few cows of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a few cows of your own, if robots can do it all by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want my children to know where milk comes from, from a cow, not a factory. And because I'd miss them. That's the honest reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the owners of Greenhill to do in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell us early what they're planning. Don't wait until the robots are on the lorry. If they're straight with us, we'll be straight with them.

S4.say: She'd say a decade means prepare, not panic, and point out that dairy farmers have adapted to quotas, prices and robots before and will again.
S4.think: She sees ten years as time to live normally, marry, buy a house and maybe have two children, then think hard about next steps around 2032.
S4.do: Marries, buys the house they wanted and starts a family when it feels right. Learns each new system once proven and buys a small piece of land near the village for a few cows of her own.
S4.quote: Because I'd want my children to know where milk comes from, from a cow, not a factory. And because I'd miss them.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Zoe's family plans go ahead in full and AI becomes a later problem. Her wish for a few cows of her own is about family and feeling, not money. She asks employers for honesty and early warning above all.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it'd land right as Mark and I are starting our life together. What would help is employers being honest early about their plans, and support for families that comes through communities and churches, not just forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the cows. People forget they're animals with moods. If robots run everything, someone still needs to care.

headlineQuote: A machine I've never seen, deciding when Mark and I have a baby.
portrait: Zoe Bauer is a 27-year-old herd manager on a dairy farm that already milks with robots, a change she resisted and then came to accept. She's traditional, engaged to a builder, planning a church wedding and a house near the village, and her answers keep returning to family plans. In the slower pictures she feels well placed and would adopt new systems once they're proven elsewhere. The two-year picture hits her hardest, shrinking the wedding, delaying a house and maybe children. With more time she pictures a bridge role between cows and engineers, and a few cows of her own.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would land just as she and her fiancé are starting their life together.
whatWouldHelp: Employers being honest early about their plans, and support for families that comes through communities and churches as well as official forms.
